Passage – 1


For more than two decades, India's information technology industry built something genuinely admirable: a world class services engine
that became the back office of the global economy. TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Tech, and Tech Mahindra collectively generated hundreds of
billions of dollars in revenue, employed millions of engineers, and powered an entire ecosystem of technical education across the country.
Then came the AI revolution - and the industry was caught almost entirely unprepared.


The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 was not a sudden shock. It was the visible peak of a transformation building since deep
learning went mainstream after 2015. But Indian IT firms, locked into low-risk service contracts and investing less than three per cent of
revenues in R&D compared to ten to twenty per cent at global technology companies, had neither the incentive nor the institutional culture
to see it coming. By the time the alarm was impossible to ignore, the frontier had already been claimed by OpenAI, Google DeepMind,
Anthropic, Meta, and a set of well-funded Chinese laboratories.


What followed was a period of genuine reckoning. The traditional pyramid model, in which armies of junior engineers churned out
standardised code with revenues scaling directly with headcount, began to crack. AI could now perform many of those base layer tasks:
routine code generation, testing, data processing, and documentation. At the same time, the growth of over 2,000 Global Capability
Centres meant multinationals that once outsourced wholesale were now building substantial in-house teams in India. The existential
question became unavoidable: if Indian IT cannot build the AI, and its traditional clients are increasingly building their own teams, what
exactly is the industry's role? Four structural failures explain why Indian IT missed the frontier AI race entirely. The first is the services trap.


(Source:The Statesman)
Q 1. Which of the following best captures the central concern of the passage?

a)
Indian IT firms built a globally respected services base but underestimated how quickly multinational clients would reduce dependence
on outsourced work.

b) Indian IT firms created a powerful services-led industry but failed to prepare for the AI-driven disruption of their own operating model.

c)
Indian IT firms became major global vendors but could not match frontier laboratories because they lacked a culture of original product
innovation.

d)
Indian IT firms expanded technical employment at scale but remained exposed when global technology companies moved ahead in
applied AI research.

Passage – 2


Feeling depressed about the state of the world? Worried about the future? You're not alone. Pessimism about politics is the new normal
among the peoples of the west. Major conflicts in Europe and the Middle East and the harms caused by right-left extremism, stagnating
economies, inequality, corruption, terrorism, racism, big tech, mass extinctions and the climate crisis make for shared nightmares.


Growing numbers of people simply refuse to personally engage with current events via the news media, finding them too anxiety-inducing
(so they probably won't be reading this). In a Reuters Institute survey last year, 40% of respondents in about 50 countries said they
sometimes or often avoid the news altogether, a rise of 29% on 2017.


Intense negativity characterises European and, to a lesser degree, North American political sentiment. In France, 90% of people questioned
by Ipsos believed their country is on the wrong track. In Britain, it was 79%; in Germany, 77%; in the US, 60%. Europeans feel similarly glum
about the bigger, global picture, unlike the Chinese, Saudis and Nigerians who are broadly upbeat, according to a GlobeScan survey.


Pew Research Center polling in 25 countries last year found that the US, Russia and China are seen, by most but not all, as the biggest
international threats. For Turks, for example, Israel is the main menace; for Greeks, it's the Turks. It gets more confusing still. Canada is
one of several countries in which majorities regard the US as both the main threat and main ally.


Disenchantment with democracy and dissatisfaction with political leaders is a ubiquitous, polarising western phenomenon. Divisions grow
entrenched. Keir Starmer, with a 27% approval rating, according to Statista, is struggling to survive. Yet Germany's chancellor, Friedrich
Merz, and France's president, Emmanuel Macron, are even less popular, on 19% and 18% respectively.


Donald Trump is down to about 38% approval, trailing his nemesis, Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, on 54%. In Russia, Vladimir
Putin's historically inflated ratings are now badly punctured. Figures for Xi Jinping are unreliable; in China, freely expressing opinions is
dangerous. India is an exception. A majority frankly adores the prime minister, Narendra Modi.


(Source: The Gurdian)
Q 6. Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?

[[PAGE 3]]
a)
Western publics are increasingly pessimistic about politics, global crises, and leadership, even as some non-Western societies remain
comparatively hopeful.

b)
Western publics are avoiding political news mainly because media coverage exaggerates global crises, leadership failures, and
democratic instability.

c) Western publics are losing trust in democracy because rival powers such as China, Russia, and the US are viewed as equal threats.

d)
Western publics are politically divided because unpopular leaders have failed to address extremism, climate change, corruption, and
economic inequality.

Passage – 3

[[PAGE 4]]
Recent diplomatic tensions between the United States and Iran have intensified after Iran responded to a U.S.-backed peace proposal with
conditions that Washington has described as "unacceptable." The proposal, aimed at ending ongoing conflict and stabilizing the region,
includes major demands such as lifting sanctions, a structured 30-day negotiation period, and nuclear-related concessions. However,
Iran's counter-response has created fresh disagreements over the terms of peace and the future of regional security.


At the centre of the dispute is Iran's demand for complete lifting of U.S. sanctions and unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad. Iran has also
insisted on an end to military pressure, including naval restrictions and blockades affecting key trade routes like the Strait of Hormuz. In
return, Iran has offered a phased approach to negotiations, suggesting that key issues, including nuclear concerns, could be resolved
within a 30-day framework. However, it has refused to dismantle its nuclear infrastructure, which remains a major point of conflict with the
U.S. proposal.


The United States, on the other hand, has pushed for stricter conditions. These include long-term limits on uranium enrichment, removal of
highly enriched uranium stockpiles, and strong verification measures. American officials argue that Iran's proposals do not go far enough
to guarantee regional stability or prevent future escalation. Former President Donald Trump, who is closely associated with the
negotiations, publicly rejected Iran's response, calling it "totally unacceptable" and warning of possible renewed military action if no
agreement is reached.


The situation has also impacted global markets and geopolitical stability. Oil prices have fluctuated due to uncertainty over the Strait of
Hormuz, a vital energy route. Meanwhile, diplomatic mediators, including Pakistan, are attempting to bridge the gap between both sides.


In conclusion, the Iran-US negotiations highlight deep mistrust and conflicting expectations. While both sides express willingness to
negotiate, differences over sanctions, nuclear policy, and regional control continue to block progress toward a lasting peace agreement.


(Source: The telegraph)

India's mental health crisis is both vast and underappreciated. According to the Global Burden of Disease study, nearly 197 million Indians -
roughly one in seven - live with some form of mental disorder. Depression and anxiety alone affect over 90 million people, yet for most,
professional support remains out of reach. For decades, stigma was considered the primary barrier. By 2025, however, the conversation
had shifted. Stigma, while still present, was no longer the central obstacle. The more urgent questions had become practical ones: how
does care actually function once someone seeks help, and what happens when symptoms escalate?


The answer, increasingly, lies in integrated, end-to-end models of care. India's mental health systems were historically built around isolated
touchpoints - therapy sessions existed separately from psychiatric care, digital tools operated independently of clinical oversight, and
hospitalisation sat at the extreme end of the spectrum, disconnected from what came before and after. Individuals and families were
expected to navigate these transitions alone, often during periods of acute vulnerability. Effective systems, experts argue, must allow
individuals to move fluidly between levels of support - digital guidance, outpatient care, crisis intervention, and structured inpatient settings
- without losing continuity of care.


Technology has played a critical role in widening access. The government's Tele-MANAS platform, upgraded in 2025 with a multilingual
interface in ten regional languages and an AI-powered chatbot named Asmi, has expanded mental health outreach significantly. Private
platforms such as Wysa, Amaha, and Lissun are using AI-driven tools to reach underserved populations. However, a key lesson from 2025
is that access alone is insufficient. Digital tools can open doors, but they cannot substitute for trained professionals or structured clinical
care.


Looking ahead, India's mental healthcare challenge in 2026 is one of consolidation rather than experimentation. Hospitals, outpatient
centres, digital platforms, workplaces, and community networks must function as parts of a coherent whole. Equally important is
recognising families not merely as informal caregivers but as active stakeholders in recovery. The opportunity is significant - India has the
chance to build a mental healthcare system that is preventative, responsive, and continuous, one that meets people where they are.

Philosophy in the Upaniṣads does not merely consist of abstract claims about the nature of reality, but is also presented as a way of living
one's life. In Yājñavalkya's teaching to Janaka, for example, knowledge of atman is associated with a change in one's disposition and
behavior. As we have seen, karma is characterized as a natural moral process, with knowledge of the self as a way out of that process. In
this respect, a fundamental assumption throughout many teachings of the self is that it is untouched by karma. Yajñavalkya teaches
Janaka that knowledge of the self is beyond virtuous (kalyana) and evil (papa)-that, through knowledge of the self one reaches the world
of brahman, where the good or bad actions of one's life do not follow.

[[PAGE 7]]
Yajñavalkya explains that in the world of brahman a thief is not a thief, a murderer is not a murderer, an outcaste not an outcaste, a mixed-
caste person (paulkasa) is not a mixed-caste person, a renunciate (sramana) is not a renunciate, and an ascetic not an ascetic, that
neither the good (punya) nor the evil (papa) follow him. In using these examples Yajñavalkya illustrates the degree to which knowledge of
the self is beyond everyday notions of moral behavior. In other words, he seems to be saying that even if one has committed evil deeds,
one can still be liberated from karma by means of knowing the self. Yet Yajñavalkya is not suggesting that one can continue to perform
'evil' deeds without suffering karmic retribution. Rather, as he asserts later in his discussion with Janaka: when one is knowledgeable, one
necessarily acts morally. Yajñavalkya explains that a man who has proper knowledge becomes calm (santa), restrained (danta), withdrawn
(uparata), patient (titiksu), and composed (samaahita). Here Yajñavalkya characterizes knowledge of the self as a change in one's
disposition. In other words, one who is a knower of the self becomes a person of good character and-by definition-would not perform an
evil action.


While Yajñavalkya talks about becoming calm, restrained, withdrawn, patient, and composed, these dispositions are not presented as
virtues to cultivate for the sake of knowledge, but rather as consequences of knowing atman. Subsequent texts would devote considerable
attention to how one should cultivate oneself in order to achieve the highest knowledge. For example, both the eight-fold path of the
Buddhist Nikayas and the eight limbs in the Yoga Sutra suggest that one needs to live a moral life in order to achieve true knowledge. In
Yajñavalkya's teaching about atman, however, there is more attention paid to the objective of knowing the self than the ethical means of
controlling the self.


(Source: https://iep.utm.edu/upanisad)

one can still be liberated from karma by means of knowing the self. Yet Yajñavalkya is not suggesting that one can continue to perform
'evil' deeds without suffering karmic retribution. Rather, as he asserts later in his discussion with Janaka: when one is knowledgeable, one
necessarily acts morally. Yajñavalkya explains that a man who has proper knowledge becomes calm (santa), restrained (danta), withdrawn

disposition. In other words, one who is a knower of the self becomes a person of good character and-by definition-would not perform an
evil action.

virtues to cultivate for the sake of knowledge, but rather as consequences of knowing atman. Subsequent texts would devote considerable

Buddhist Nikayas and the eight limbs in the Yoga Sutra suggest that one needs to live a moral life in order to achieve true knowledge. In

Mission Drishti, the world's first OptoSAR satellite developed by Bengaluru based space startup GalaxEye has been successfully launched
on May 3, 2026 aboard a Falcon 9 by SpaceX from Vandenberg, California. Weighing 190 kilograms, Mission Drishti is India's largest
privately developed Earth observation satellite. "It is the first satellite globally to integrate Electro-Optical (EO) and Synthetic Aperture
Radar (SAR) sensors into a single operational platform, enabling all-weather, day-and-night imaging capabilities. This integrated approach
addresses long-standing limitations of conventional systems and enables more reliable and consistent data acquisition across diverse
environmental conditions," GalaxEye said. "Mission Drishti marks our first mission and the culmination of over five years of sustained R&D
to develop this breakthrough technology. With the satellite now successfully in orbit, our immediate focus is on completing its
commissioning. As we move through this phase, we are already witnessing strong global interest in the differentiated datasets enabled by
our OptoSAR payload." said Suyash Singh, Founder & CEO, GalaxEye. Following its successful deployment and commissioning initial
imagery is expected to be delivered to customers in the coming weeks. GalaxEye said that the satellite has already generated significant
interest from government and commercial stakeholders internationally, seeking access to high-quality, high-frequency Earth observation
data. On the successful launch, Dr. Pawan Goenka, Chairman, Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center (IN-SPACe) said
that the sustained effort over the last five to six years on confidence-building, capacity-building and the commercialisation of India's
private space technology ecosystem is now showing tangible results. "Mission Drishti by GalaxEye is a fine example of this - the world's
first OptoSAR satellite from an Indian private player. As more Indian space companies demonstrate their capabilities through real missions
and engagement with global customers, confidence in India's space ecosystem will continue to strengthen, creating greater demand both
in India and overseas. I compliment the GalaxEye team on this important milestone and wish them continued success," said Dr. Goenka.
Mission Drishti is a dual-use Earth observation Satellite, supporting use cases across defence, agriculture, disaster management, maritime
monitoring, and infrastructure planning. The satellite is expected to complement India's broader initiatives, including the active 29 Earth
Observation satellites outlined in ISRO's recent annual report.

International Humanitarian Law (IHL), also referred to as the law of armed conflict or the law of war, consists of rules intended to limit the
effects of armed conflict for humanitarian reasons. Rather than determining whether a war itself is lawful, IHL regulates conduct during
armed conflict and seeks to balance military necessity with humanitarian considerations. Its primary objectives are to protect persons
who are not, or are no longer, participating in hostilities and to restrict methods and means of warfare that cause unnecessary suffering.


IHL principally applies during international and non-international armed conflicts. Among its most fundamental principles is the principle
of distinction, which requires parties to a conflict to distinguish at all times between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects
and military objectives. Attacks may lawfully be directed only against military objectives. Civilian persons and civilian objects, such as
schools, hospitals, and homes, cannot ordinarily be targeted merely because incidental military advantage may arise from their
destruction. Closely related is the principle of proportionality, which prohibits attacks expected to cause incidental civilian harm that would
be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. This principle does not prohibit all civilian casualties;
rather, it seeks to prevent disproportionate harm. Even where a legitimate military objective exists, military operations must not impose
excessive burdens on civilians.


The principle of military necessity permits only those measures necessary to achieve a legitimate military objective and not otherwise
prohibited by international law. However, military necessity does not override all humanitarian obligations. Certain weapons and practices
remain prohibited because they cause unnecessary suffering or fail to distinguish between military and civilian targets. Thus, military
convenience cannot justify every action during war. Another important principle is humanity, which prohibits means and methods of
warfare causing superfluous injury or unnecessary suffering. Torture, cruel treatment, collective punishment, and attacks directed
primarily to spread terror among civilians are generally prohibited. Persons who are wounded, detained, or otherwise hors de combat (out
of combat) are entitled to humane treatment irrespective of nationality or allegiance.


The law also recognises the protection of medical personnel and humanitarian workers. Hospitals and medical units generally enjoy
special protection because they serve humanitarian functions. However, such protection may cease if these facilities are used, outside
their humanitarian purpose, for acts harmful to the enemy, though reasonable warning may be required before protection is withdrawn.
Violations of serious IHL obligations may amount to war crimes. However, superior orders do not automatically excuse unlawful conduct.
Individuals may bear responsibility where they knowingly participate in grave violations of humanitarian norms.

functioning school over three consecutive days to relay troop coordinates. The school's lower floors continue to be used by
approximately 200 students and remain in regular operation. The school is located near an active front line. Acting on this intelligence
but without conducting a proportionality assessment or issuing any civilian warning, State X launches sustained missile strikes that
destroy the entire building during school hours, causing extensive civilian casualties. Which of the following is the most appropriate
conclusion?

a)
The attack is lawful because credible, repeated military use of a structure by enemy forces is sufficient under IHL to classify it as a
military objective, and the principle of military necessity permits its destruction irrespective of continued civilian occupation.

b)

c)
The attack may be permissible because military necessity allows commanders to act decisively on confirmed intelligence of repeated
military use, and the school's proximity to an active front line further diminishes its ordinary civilian character.

d)
The attack appears unlawful because targeting a building with substantial civilian occupancy through sustained strikes, without
proportionality assessment or civilian warning, likely violates both the principle of distinction and the principle of proportionality.

Constitutional democracies ordinarily distribute governmental authority among different institutions to prevent concentration of power in a
single body. This arrangement is reflected in the doctrine of separation of powers, under which legislative bodies generally enact laws, the

rigid or absolute division of functions. Modern constitutional systems often permit a degree of overlap because complete separation may
be impractical. Nevertheless, the central purpose remains to ensure checks and balances so that no organ exercises uncontrolled power.

courts to examine the validity of legislative enactments and executive actions and determine whether they conform to constitutional
requirements. Courts exercising judicial review do not ordinarily assess whether a law is wise, economically beneficial, or politically
desirable. Rather, they examine whether constitutional limitations have been violated. Thus, disagreement with legislative policy is distinct
from constitutional invalidity. At the same time, courts generally recognise that elected branches possess institutional competence in
certain areas involving policy decisions, economic regulation, allocation of resources, and matters requiring specialised expertise.
Therefore, judicial restraint is sometimes considered appropriate where constitutional rights are not directly threatened. However, judicial
restraint does not imply judicial abdication. Courts may intervene where governmental actions are arbitrary, violate constitutional
guarantees, exceed legal authority, or undermine fundamental rights.


The doctrine of checks and balances recognises that constitutional organs may possess limited powers to review or influence one

[[PAGE 17]]
another. Such interaction does not necessarily destroy separation of powers. For instance, executive actions may require legislative
approval, legislation may be subject to constitutional scrutiny by courts, and certain appointments or actions may involve more than one

alone cannot justify actions violating fundamental rights. Constitutional guarantees often exist precisely to protect individuals and
minority groups from excessive exercises of governmental power.

The law may withstand challenge because prior regulatory frameworks for media content fall within the institutional competence of

Courts may appropriately examine the law because judicial review permits scrutiny of whether legislative enactments conform to

A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. It ordinarily
involves three parties: the principal debtor, who is primarily liable for the debt or obligation; the creditor, to whom the obligation is owed;
and the surety, who undertakes to discharge the liability if the principal debtor fails to do so. The liability of the surety is generally co-
extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless otherwise provided by the contract. This means that the surety may be called upon to
satisfy the same obligation that the principal debtor was bound to perform.


Unlike ordinary contracts, consideration in a contract of guarantee may consist of any act, promise, or benefit done for the benefit of the
principal debtor. It is not necessary that the surety receive direct consideration personally. However, a valid guarantee requires free
consent, and if consent is obtained through misrepresentation or concealment of material facts, the guarantee may become invalid. For
instance, if the creditor deliberately suppresses information regarding the financial condition or conduct of the principal debtor and such
information would have influenced the surety's decision, the guarantee may be affected.


Guarantees may be specific or continuing. A specific guarantee applies to a single transaction or obligation and comes to an end once that
transaction is completed. A continuing guarantee, however, extends to a series of transactions and remains operative until revoked or
otherwise terminated according to law. A continuing guarantee may be revoked by the surety concerning future transactions through
notice to the creditor. However, such revocation does not affect transactions that have already occurred before the notice was given.
Further, the death of a surety ordinarily operates as revocation of a continuing guarantee with respect to future transactions, unless there
exists a contract providing otherwise.


The law also recognises certain circumstances under which the surety may be discharged from liability. A surety may be discharged if the
creditor and principal debtor enter into a contract varying the terms of the original agreement without the surety's consent, where the
creditor releases the principal debtor, or where the creditor acts in a manner impairing the surety's eventual remedies against the principal
debtor. Such discharge may occur because the surety agreed to guarantee only a specific obligation and should not be subjected to
materially altered risks without consent. After satisfying the debt, the surety acquires certain rights against the principal debtor. This
principle, often referred to as subrogation, permits the surety to step into the shoes of the creditor and exercise the rights that the creditor
could have exercised against the principal debtor. The surety may also claim indemnification from the principal debtor for amounts
rightfully paid under the guarantee.

The law of tort recognises that a person may not always be held liable for damage merely because harm has occurred. Certain
circumstances may excuse liability where the defendant demonstrates that the event occurred despite the exercise of reasonable care
and caution. Two closely related yet distinct concepts in this regard are inevitable accident and Act of God (Vis Major). Although both may
relieve a defendant from liability, they differ in their origin and legal requirements.


An inevitable accident refers to an occurrence which could not have been prevented despite the exercise of reasonable care, caution, and
skill by the defendant. The central inquiry is not whether the event caused damage, but whether a reasonable and prudent person
exercising ordinary care could have avoided it. The event may arise from human conduct, mechanical failure, or unforeseen
circumstances. However, the defendant cannot rely upon inevitable accident where negligence, omission, or lack of proper precautions
contributed to the occurrence. Thus, a person who fails to inspect equipment, ignores warning signs, or neglects ordinary safety measures
cannot later claim that the accident was inevitable.


An Act of God, on the other hand, is a natural event arising exclusively from forces of nature that are so extraordinary and unforeseeable
that no amount of human foresight or reasonable care could prevent the resulting damage. Examples may include unprecedented floods,
earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or violent natural disturbances. The natural event must operate independently of human intervention and
must be so unusual that it could not reasonably have been anticipated. Ordinary seasonal rainfall, predictable weather conditions, or
recurring natural events generally do not qualify merely because they cause harm.


The distinction between these principles becomes important where natural events and human conduct combine. If a natural event merely
contributes to the damage but human negligence substantially contributes to the loss, liability may still arise. Conversely, where the
defendant exercised reasonable care and the damage was solely attributable to an extraordinary natural force, the defence of Act of God
may succeed. The burden generally lies upon the defendant to establish facts supporting these defences. Further, where a defendant
voluntarily undertakes a hazardous activity or introduces potentially dangerous things into their control, courts may closely examine
whether reasonable precautions proportionate to the risk were adopted.

Criminal liability generally arises where an individual directly commits an offence. However, the law also recognises that a person may be
held responsible even without personally carrying out the prohibited act. This principle is reflected in the law relating to abetment, which
seeks to punish conduct encouraging, facilitating, or assisting the commission of an offence. The rationale is that a person who
deliberately contributes to the commission of an offence may be as blameworthy as the person physically committing it.


Abetment may arise in three principal ways: instigation, conspiracy, and intentional aiding. Though these concepts may overlap in certain
situations, they are distinct in their legal requirements. Instigation refers to actively provoking, urging, inciting, encouraging, or stimulating
another person to commit an act. Such encouragement may be express or implied and may occur through words, conduct, written
communication, or even deliberate omission in certain circumstances. However, mere casual remarks, expressions of anger, or
statements lacking intention to provoke commission of an offence may not amount to instigation. The focus lies upon whether the
accused intended to influence or encourage another person toward committing the act. Abetment by conspiracy occurs where two or

[[PAGE 23]]
more persons agree to commit an unlawful act or agree to commit a lawful act through unlawful means, and some act or illegal omission
takes place in furtherance of that agreement. Mere knowledge of an unlawful plan or passive association with conspirators does not by
itself constitute conspiracy. There must ordinarily exist a meeting of minds and some step taken toward execution of the common design.
Abetment by intentional aiding occurs where a person intentionally facilitates commission of an offence through acts or omissions. Aid
may take various forms, including providing tools, information, transport, shelter, or any other assistance that substantially contributes to
the offence. Mere presence at the scene of occurrence does not necessarily amount to aiding unless accompanied by conduct intended to
facilitate commission of the offence. A person may be liable for abetment even if the principal offence ultimately differs in manner from
what was originally intended, provided the consequences are a probable result of the conduct encouraged or assisted. However, where the
principal offender acts independently and outside the scope of what was instigated or facilitated, liability for abetment may not arise.

operations. To address these concerns, the consultant organized meetings with managers, explained the long-term benefits of
coordination, and encouraged employees to provide suggestions before changes were implemented.

competitive market.
